title: Friday the 13th: Why Does This Day Scare So Many People?
summary:
Friday, November 13, 2026, is the third and last Friday the 13th of the year. For most people, it is simply the start of the weekend. But for millions of people around the world, it can feel like the unluckiest day of the year. Some even have a name for the fear: paraskevidekatriaphobia, the extreme fear of Friday the 13th.

No one knows exactly how the belief began, but several theories point to the number 13. Professor Thomas Fernsler of the University of Delaware notes that 13 gets a bad reputation because it comes right after the number 12, which many people see as complete: 12 months in a year, 12 zodiac signs, and 12 apostles of Jesus. Because 13 follows that tidy number, it often feels incomplete, and therefore unlucky.

Folklore historian Donald Dossey traces the fear to a Norse myth from the Viking era. According to the legend, twelve gods were enjoying a peaceful dinner when Loki, the god of mischief, arrived uninvited and tricked Hodr, the blind god of darkness, into killing Baldr, the god of joy and light. Many Nordic cultures still consider 13 guests at a table unlucky, and in France, some people hire a 14th guest to avoid the number.

According to the Bible, Jesus was crucified on a Friday, shortly after the Last Supper, which included 13 people. People who fear the day may feel anything from mild anxiety to full panic.

Surprisingly, the day also affects the United States economy: businesses lose as much as $900 million when people avoid work, travel, or big purchases. Yet a 2008 Dutch study found fewer traffic accidents that day than on other Fridays. For bargain hunters, special discounts might turn the last Friday the 13th of 2026 into your luckiest day yet.
why_it_matters: The fear of Friday the 13th shows how old stories and beliefs can still shape how millions of people feel and act today, even costing businesses as much as $900 million. Understanding where such fears come from helps us tell the difference between superstition and real risk.

background_read: Friday the 13th is a day many people treat as unlucky, and some people feel real fear when it arrives. Much of that fear comes from the number 13, which follows 12, a number many people see as complete because a year has 12 months and there are 12 signs of the zodiac. Old stories added to the fear: a Norse myth tells of a dinner with twelve gods that turned tragic when an uninvited thirteenth guest arrived, and the Bible tells of a Last Supper with thirteen people before Jesus was crucified on a Friday. Over time these stories mixed together, so the day became a symbol of bad luck that can make people nervous or change their plans, even though nothing about the date itself causes bad things to happen.
